key_insight: Two automated speech measures—Nasal Cognate Distinctiveness (NCD) and nasal posterior probability (NPP)—both track hypernasality in motor speech disorders and perform similarly for identifying clinically meaningful nasality.
clinical_relevance: These metrics could help provide objective, scalable support for assessing hypernasality in patients with motor speech disorders, complementing clinician ratings.
method: 561 speech recordings: 374 neurologically typical controls and 187 patients with motor speech disorders
Compared NCD on voiceless stops (/p/, /t/, /k/) with NPP from a phonological-feature neural network across stops, consonants, and vowels
Used clinician hypernasality ratings plus mixed-effects models, Spearman correlations, ROC analysis, and test-retest reliability
evidence_signal: Both measures showed strong relationships with hypernasality severity and similar discrimination of absent vs present hypernasality (NCD AUC 0.796; NPP AUC 0.730), while consonant and vowel NPP both reached AUC 0.853.
watch_item: Results come from a single dataset and the measures showed some test-retest variability, so local validation and careful threshold setting would be needed before routine use.
paper_title: Automated Assessment of Hypernasality in Motor Speech Disorders Using Nasal Cognate Distinctiveness and Nasal Posterior Probability
